¶ The theory of "Leaves of Grass," as an utterance or composition of verses, we are authentically informed, has been ‸from first to last to thoroughly possess the mind, memory, cognizance of the author ‸himself with everything beforehand, a full armory of ‸concrete actualities, observations, humanity, past poems, ballads, facts, ‸technique war and peace, politics, north and south, easte and west, ‸nothing too large or too small, the sciences as ‸far as possible—and above all, America and the present— —after and out of which the subject of the poem, long or short, has been ‸invariably turned over to thehis emotionality, even thehis Personality, to be is shaped thence; and thence emerges ‸with all its merits and demerits on its head. Every page ‸of Walt Whitman's poetry therefore smacks of the living ‸physical identity date, environment, individuality, probably beyond any thing known, and ‸in a style often offensively to the conventions. ¶ This new last little cluster "Good⹀Bye my Fancy," follows suit and yet with a difference. The clef is here changed to its lowest, and its it ‸this little book is a lot of tremulos ab't old age, death and faith, ‸the physical just lingers, but almost vanishes. It is garrulous, irascible (like old Lear) and has various breaks and even tricks to avoid monotony.—and is It will have to be ciphered out long—and is in some respects the most curious part of its author's curious works.
